newsitem.title: THAILAND: Little scope seen for Thai rate cuts by year - end.
newsitem.headline: Little scope seen for Thai rate cuts by year - end.

text.p: Chances of a meaningful cut in high Thai interest rates by year-end look slim given intense competition for local deposits and the need to attract foreign capital, bankers and analysts said on Thursday.

"The scenario has changed now from two months ago," said Sataporn Janichatra, executive vice-president at Siam Commercial Bank. He was referring to forecasts by government advisors and some private forecasters in July that a 100-150 basis point cut in rates by 1997 was possible.
But many analysts said they now expected rates to remain steady until the end of the year, with some expecting no more than a maximum cut of 25 basis points if rates softened.
"For the next one or two months I think stimulating the economy is not high on their (the central bank's) agenda. I think stability is," Sataporn said.
The minimum lending rate is 13.25 percent, one of the highest in the region.
The formerly robust Thai economy has slowed, with authorities and analysts expecting gross domestic product growth (GDP) to be well below the 8.6 percent recorded in 1995.

Thailand is also going through a politically volatile period, with a change in prime minister and cabinet likely by the end of the week. Outgoing premier Banharn Silpa-archa is to quit by Saturday and markets are awaiting his replacement.

"I don't see that real interest rates can really be cut," said Youssef Abboud, analyst with Wall Street Finance and Securities Plc. "They must remain high to keep foreign money coming in to finance the current account deficit."
The current account deficit, which ran at 8.1 percent of GDP last year, remains high.

Central bank balance of payments data for July suggests a net outflow of foreign funds. Double-digit rates in the overnight interbank market over the past two months have pushed up borrowing costs for smaller banks, and suggest capital inflows have slowed.

Kanjanee Kangwanporisi, assistant Managing Director at Thai Fuji, said recent lending restrictions imposed by the central bank on offshore borrowing would keep liquidity tight. She predicted a rate cut of no more than 25 basis points towards the end of the year.
With Moody's downgrade pushing up offshore borrowing costs, competition between banks for domestic deposits remains intense, analysts said.
Recently, Bank of Ayudhya, Thai Danu Bank and Bank of Asia raised most fixed-term deposit rates by 25 basis points.
Wall Street Finance's Abboud said rising deposit rates meant bank lending rates should remain high to cover increased costs.

"We are running into a dilemma between high and low interest rates: Whether to kickstart industry, or keep rates high," said a senior analyst at Thai Farmers Bank Research Centre. "I don't see rates coming down but I do see them holding level."

A senior bond trader at Nava Finance and Securities Plc said the local debt market had already realised that interest rates cannot be cut in the short term and yields have risen by up to 100 basis points in the last two weeks.
